Chapter 3: The Power of Unpredictable Events and the Limits of Prediction.
Every now and then, life throws something at us that nobody could’ve expected. Maybe it’s a new technology that changes the way we live, a sudden crisis that shakes entire communities, or even a single, random encounter that shifts someone’s entire path. Moments like these—rare, powerful, and totally unpredictable—remind us that the future just isn’t as clear as we’d like to think.
Picture this: there’s a small business owner who’s feeling pretty good about their steady progress. Then, out of nowhere, a new competitor shows up. Overnight, the whole landscape changes. All those years of careful planning suddenly feel worthless. The owner scrambles to adjust, realizing that sometimes, it’s the risks you couldn’t possibly have seen coming that change everything.
We’re all taught to believe that with enough information, we can figure out what’s ahead. Experts build fancy models, analysts pour over endless data, and everyone takes comfort in that sense of certainty. But if you look back at history, you’ll see event after event that nobody saw coming—wars, market crashes, scientific breakthroughs. These are what some call “Black Swan” events. And honestly, they shape the world way more than the slow, predictable stuff ever could.
It’s so tempting to look back and say, “You know, the signs were there. Someone should’ve seen it coming.” But that’s just us trying to hang on to the idea that we’re in control. In reality, the biggest moments are often invisible until they hit.
Take a teacher, for example, looking back on years in the classroom. Maybe there was a student who seemed pretty average—nothing special. Fast forward a few years, and that same student is making a real difference in the world, maybe even changing lives. Nobody, not the teacher, not the student, could’ve predicted that outcome. And that’s just another sign that the future is packed with surprises, some good, some not so much.
Trying to guess every twist and turn? It’s exhausting, and honestly, it doesn’t work. A smarter way is to build your life—and your systems—so they can handle shocks. Make them strong enough to weather surprises. This isn’t about guessing what’s next, but about knowing that surprises are just part of the deal.
There’s a kind of peace that comes from letting go of the urge to know everything in advance. It opens space for flexibility, creativity, and maybe even the chance to be pleasantly surprised. In the end, what really shapes our world are the things nobody could have seen coming—and maybe, that’s what makes life so interesting.
